ObjectName.value: Early Medieval Buckle

Categories.value: Portable Antiquities Scheme|Images uploaded by Fæ|Early Medieval buckles in the Portable Antiquities Scheme|Hoards in the Portable Antiquities Scheme|Portable Antiquities Scheme, NMS|Early Medieval belt buckles in the Portable Antiquities Scheme

Artist.value: Norfolk Museums Service, Mary Chester-Kadwell, 2012-05-28 14:35:45

ImageDescription.value:
Incomplete medieval gilded copper-alloy buckle frame. Part only of the cast openwork broad angled outside edge with vertical curling lobed tendrils between two robed seated figures. Both sides of the frame, the pin and the probably integral plate, are missing. The figures, both male, have their heads slightly inclined towards one another, as if in conversation. Both faces are worn, as are other exposed elements, with no surviving features although some indication of hairstyle remains. The left hand figure has both hands on his right knee which is raised and projects forward with his foot placed on a globular knop at one end of the convex outside edge. The other figure's right arm is bent with his elbow angled towards the central tendril and with his right hand on his right knee. His left hand is placed on his left knee and his left foot rests on a globular knop at the other end of the outside edge. Stumps of the broken openwork frame survive at the outside edge of both figures. Surviving length 22 mm. Surviving width 33 mm. Weighs 13.40 g.

This remarkable buckle frame is paralleled by a silver gilt example found in the Dune Hoard, Gotland (Swarzenski, Monuments fig. 535). which has been dated to c. 1200. For a discussion of the significance of this object see Heslop, T.A., and Ashley, S., 2013 'A fragment of a gilt bronze buckle frame from Soham, Cambridgeshire, and the Dune Hoard belt buckle in Stockholm' Antiquaries Journal 93, 1-7 .

ObjectName.value: Medieval Buckle Plate

Categories.value: Portable Antiquities Scheme|Images uploaded by Fæ|Buckle plates in the Portable Antiquities Scheme|Portable Antiquities Scheme, SF

Artist.value: Suffolk County Council Archaeology Service, Andrew Brown, 2009-02-18 12:50:24

ImageDescription.value:
An incomplete and worn copper alloy Medieval buckle plate. It is flat, rectangular in plan and is missing part of the frame end/pin slot, and any back/bottom plate that may once have existed, due to old breaks. At the attachment end are two circular perforations for attachment to a belt or strap, while at the opposite end the plate has square frame recesses and a rectangular pin slot. Two short integral rectangular projections mark the beginnings of loops that would have held in place the now missing buckle frame, one of which has been bent upwards probably as a result of damage whilst in the ground. The remainder of the plate missing due to old breaks. The front face of the plate is decorated with moulded and gilded relief work. This consists of a recessed border that possibly contains rocker decoration or similar moulded relief work. Within the border are three figures. The central figure is seated and to either side are standing figures that face the central figure with their arms raised towards his head. All three figures are of similar height, with globular heads just breaching the border, but the finer details of the figures are lost due to post-depositional wear. Traces of gilding can be seen on all the exterior faces of the plate, and in very small quantity on the otherwise undecorated back face. The plate measures 32.15mm in width, 20.83mm in height, 2.34mm in thickness, and weighs 5.25g.

It remains slightly uncertain as to who the figures are that are depicted on the front of this buckle plate. Parallels from Norfolk (NMS-BE78A6 and NMS-4655A1) and Denbighshire (LANCUM-193FE7) recorded through the Portable Antiquities Scheme indicate that this example is of Medieval date, probably dating between the 12th and 14th centuries AD. However, two differing interpretations of the figures are given. On the one hand (see LANCUM-193FE7), it is possible that they represent Christ with his parents or 'Christ in Majesty' (Christ seated and flanked by his mother Mary and a patron saint or angel). Contrastingly, it is also possible that the seated figure represents a King, perhaps during his coronation, hence the flanking figures with arms raised towards his head (see NMS-BE78A6 and NMS-4655A1). Due to the preservation of the current example it remains uncertain as to which explanation is correct, although both are equally plausible.

The closest parallel, characterised by a wider border than on most examples, was found close by, at Bury St Edmunds, and can be found illustrated in Cherry (1987, Pl. XXXIIb).
